issues.legal_issue: An unregistered instrument that itself allocates specific immovable properties among co-parceners cannot prove title to those properties or that they ceased to be joint property, but may prove an intention to separate in status.
material_facts: In a partition proceeding, the parties relied on a written instrument that allocated specific parcels of land and portions of a house among the co-parceners.
issues.conclusion: The instrument required registration and was inadmissible to prove title to any particular property or that any property had ceased to be joint property. It was admissible to prove the parties’ intention to become divided in status.
issues.legal_principle: Section 17(1)(b) of the Registration Act requires registration of an instrument that creates or declares rights in immovable property by allocating specific properties. Under Nanni Bai v. Gita Bai, an unregistered instrument of this kind may nevertheless be used to show severance of joint status, but not to establish rights in specific properties or their partition.

predicates.partition_proceeding: The parties were litigating a division of jointly held family property.
predicates.unregistered_partition_instrument: A party relied on a written instrument that had not been registered.
predicates.instrument_allocates_specific_immovable_: The instrument assigned identified immovable properties to particular co-parceners.
predicates.instrument_admissible_only_to_prove_seve: The instrument may be used to show that the co-parceners intended to separate in status, but not to prove rights in particular properties or that those properties ceased to be joint.

issues.definition: When an unregistered instrument in a partition proceeding assigns specific immovable properties to particular co-parceners, it may establish severance of status but not the specific property allocations.

issues.legal_issue: A party cannot rely on acquiescence as a ground to defeat a claim when that ground was not pleaded and no issue on it was framed.
material_facts: A party argued that a signatory had acquiesced in a division of property by signing the instrument and not challenging it for a period of years.
The party had not pleaded acquiescence, and the trial court had framed no issue on it.
issues.conclusion: The party could not set up the plea of acquiescence, and the finding that the signatory had relinquished her share on that basis was erroneous.
issues.legal_principle: A party may not obtain a decision on a factual plea that was neither raised in the pleadings nor made an issue for trial.

predicates.partition_proceeding: The parties were litigating a division of jointly held family property.
predicates.acquiescence_raised_without_pleading: A party argued that another party had accepted a property division by conduct, although the argument had not been pleaded.
predicates.no_issue_framed_on_acquiescence: The court did not frame an issue for trial on whether the alleged conduct amounted to acquiescence.

issues.definition: In a partition proceeding, a party cannot rely on alleged acquiescence when it was not pleaded and no issue on it was framed.

issues.legal_issue: The eldest son is not entitled to a larger share merely under the doctrine of Jethansi, and a special family custom supporting a larger share must be established by proper evidence.
material_facts: In a partition proceeding, the eldest son claimed a larger share based on the asserted custom of Jethansi in the family’s community.
The evidence about the asserted custom was vague and conflicting, and no documentary evidence of the custom or relevant partitions was produced.
issues.conclusion: The claim to a larger share was rejected because the asserted custom had not been established. The doctrine of Jethansi was obsolete and unenforceable; equality of division applied.
issues.legal_principle: The governing principle of Hindu law is equality of division, and the former special share for the eldest son under Jethansi or Jeshtbhagam is obsolete and unenforceable. A special family custom to the contrary may be recognised only if proved; a custom must be ancient, certain and reasonable and, as a departure from the general rule, is construed strictly. The Court referred to M. Y. A. A. Nachiappa Chettiar v. M. Y. A. A. Muthu Karuppan Chettiar and Hur Purshad v. Sheo Dyal.

predicates.partition_proceeding: The parties were litigating a division of jointly held family property.
predicates.eldest_son_claimed_extra_share_under_cus: The eldest son sought a greater share than the other family members on the basis of an asserted family or community custom.
predicates.custom_evidence_vague_or_conflicting: The evidence offered to establish the asserted custom was uncertain or conflicting and did not reliably establish its practice.

issues.definition: In a partition proceeding, an eldest son’s claim to an extra share based on custom is rejected when the evidence offered to establish that custom is vague or conflicting.

issues.legal_issue: Oral evidence cannot prove a subsequent partition when the parties intended an unregistered instrument to be the sole evidence of the partition and the instrument cannot establish the property allocations.
material_facts: In a partition proceeding, the parties intended the written instrument to be the sole evidence of their partition.
The instrument was unregistered and allocated specific properties.
A party offered oral evidence that a partition with specific allotments occurred after the instrument was executed.
issues.conclusion: The oral evidence was inadmissible to prove a subsequent partition.
issues.legal_principle: Section 91 of the Evidence Act bars oral evidence of the terms of a transaction when those terms have been reduced to a document intended to be the sole evidence of them. Because the unregistered instrument could not establish the specific property partition, oral evidence could not be used to prove a later partition in the circumstances of this case.

predicates.partition_proceeding: The parties were litigating a division of jointly held family property.
predicates.partition_instrument_intended_as_sole_ev: The parties intended a written instrument to be the sole evidence of their property partition.
predicates.unregistered_instrument_unusable_to_prov: The instrument was unregistered and assigned specific properties, so it could not establish the particular property allocations.
predicates.oral_evidence_offered_to_prove_later_par: A party offered oral testimony that specific property allotments were made in a later partition.

issues.definition: When a partition instrument is intended to be the sole evidence of the partition but cannot establish the specific property allocations, oral evidence offered to prove a later partition is inadmissible.
